title: Raga Sarang
hookLine: a raga for the hot middle of the day, and a Guru who calls himself a servant

cards: Noon on a hot street. The shadow of a lamppost has shrunk to a dark puddle at its foot. Phones buzz, inboxes fill, and the day is at its loudest, half gone and half still to do.
The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition gives to this hot, bright middle. It's called Sarang. So what does its first hymn do with the busiest part of the day?

teach.h: AFTER BASANT: THE HEAT OF THE DAY.
teach.b: Sarang follows Basant in the Granth's order, so the book moves from spring to the heat of the day.
Tradition sings it in the midday hours, and later in the section there's also a Var, a ballad of stanzas with saloks between them, by Guru Ram Das.
The section opens with a hymn of Guru Nanak, and its first line is a surprise from a Guru.

teach.h: I AM THE SERVANT OF MY OWN MASTER.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I am the servant girl of my own Master.

teach.h: HOLDING THE FEET, EGO AT REST.
teach.b: I have taken hold of the feet of God, the life of the world, and my ego has been settled and put to rest.

In the Granth the Gurus sometimes speak in the voice of a bride or a servant before God, and here the picture is of someone who has stopped running the house and simply holds on to the Master. Now set that at noon.
Midday is when the self is busiest: deciding, answering, pushing the list along. It's the easiest hour to feel in charge of everything.

The opening of Sarang puts a different picture at its center: not someone on top of the day, but someone holding the feet of the One who gives the world its life, with the ego quiet. That doesn't mean stopping work.
In the hymn's picture the work goes on, but the house has a Master, and it isn't the servant.
A shadow at noon is small, because the sun is right overhead. The hymn's ego is small for the same reason.

how: In kirtan, shabads from the Sarang section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Sarang, which tradition associates with the midday hours, and the Var of Sarang is sung or read in the sangat.

games.q: it's noon and everything is on you. in Sarang's opening hymn, where does Guru Nanak put himself?
o: in charge of the whole house.
as a servant holding the Master's feet.
outside, away from all of it.
games.why: the hymn says: I am the servant of my own Master; I've taken hold of the feet of God, and my ego is put to rest.

practice: Wherever you are in the day, stop what you're running for a minute: put your hands down, palms open, as if you've set down the keys to the whole operation, and if it's near noon, let a shabad in Raga Sarang play.

Breathe slowly, notice how much of you was busy being in charge, and let some of it rest. If you pray, hold Guru Nanak's picture of holding the Master's feet; if you don't, simply let the open hands do the work.

wordCard.voice: Raga Sarang. The midday raga after Basant, opening with Guru Nanak as the servant of his own Master, his ego at rest. Today's word.

orig.note: sarang, the midday raga that follows Basant in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: midday. In Sarang's first hymn, the work goes on, but the house has a Master. Back tomorrow, same hill.
